opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difficulty is that video is enormously rich but extremely inefficient as a training signal. Compare it with text. Every token in text has been compressed by a human. Someone already decided what was worth saying, so the information density is very high. Video is the opposite. You get thirty frames a second, and most of them are nearly identical. The meaningful change, the part that actually tells you something about the world, is a tiny fraction of the raw pixels. So the first problem is simply compute and density. You spend a huge budget processing data where most of the bits are redundant.

The second problem, and I think the deeper one, is that we don't have a good objective for video the way next-token prediction works for language. In language, predicting the next word forces the model to learn grammar, facts and even some reasoning, because language is already an abstraction. If you predict the next frame at the pixel level, the model spends most of its capacity on texture, lighting and noise, things that are hard to predict and don't matter much for understanding. People have tried predicting in latent space, or using masked modeling, or aligning video with captions. Each helps somewhat, but none has shown the clean scaling behavior we saw with text, where more data and more compute reliably give you more intelligence.

Third, there's the question of what the model actually learns. Ideally, from watching video you'd learn physics, causality, how objects persist, how agents behave. In practice, models are very good at finding shortcuts. They learn appearance statistics, or they lean on the paired text, and the visual understanding stays shallow. When you train with video-text pairs, the text is often low quality, like titles, ASR transcripts or auto-generated captions, and it describes only a small part of what's happening. So the supervision is weak and noisy.

Finally, there's the tension between understanding and generation. Generation models have made huge progress, and the videos look amazing. That doesn't automatically mean the representation is useful for reasoning or understanding. Unifying the two, so that the model generating the video is also the one that understands it, is still an open problem. My view is that video will matter a lot in the long run, especially for embodied intelligence and world models. But right now the bottleneck isn't the amount of data. It's that we haven't found the right way to turn that data into intelligence efficiently.

r001.rationale: The response says video-paired text is often low quality and describes only a small part of the video, but it does not compare that language content with interleaved image-text corpora.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the fundamental problem with video is that the information density is extremely low. If you take a video and look at it frame by frame, adjacent frames are nearly identical, and over a minute of footage the amount of genuinely new information might be equivalent to a few sentences of text. So compared with text, where every token carries meaning, video is a very "dilute" signal. You spend an enormous amount of compute just to process redundancy.

The second difficulty is that video doesn't come with a natural supervision signal. Text has next-token prediction, and that works because language is already a compressed, abstract representation of the world. Pixels aren't. If you do next-frame prediction, the model mostly learns low-level things, such as how textures move and how lighting changes, rather than the causal structure of what's happening. The question of what you should actually predict in video, in what representation space, is still unresolved.

And then there's the alignment problem. Most video on the internet has very weak captions, or captions describing something unrelated to what's on screen. For images, the web gave us a huge pile of roughly aligned image-text pairs. For video, that pairing is far noisier, and the temporal part, which is exactly what makes video valuable, is almost never described in text at all. Nobody writes "at second twelve the cup falls off the table."

So the way I look at it, the difficulty isn't getting the data. There's plenty of video. The difficulty is extracting the small amount of real knowledge inside it at a cost that makes sense, and finding a learning objective that pushes the model toward understanding dynamics and causality instead of just memorizing appearance. Until we solve that, video will be an expensive supplement to text rather than a replacement for it.

r001.rationale: The response says video captions are often weak or unrelated and rarely describe temporal events, contrasting them with the roughly aligned image-text pairs available for images.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difficulty is that a video contains a lot of information, but it doesn’t necessarily come with language that explains that information. The audio might describe something that isn’t on screen, and important visual events might never be mentioned. So simply pairing frames with a transcript doesn’t give you clean multimodal supervision.

There’s also the temporal dimension. If you sample too few frames, you can miss the action or the relationship between events. If you keep everything, the computational cost becomes very high, and much of what you process is redundant. The challenge is to preserve the meaningful changes over time and connect them to the right language.

r001.rationale: The response says video audio or transcripts may omit visual information, but it does not state that video corpora have less rich accompanying language than interleaved image-text corpora.

sol-6.1.text: I think the main difficulty is turning raw video into useful, well-aligned training data. A video contains images, speech, text, and motion, but those signals don’t necessarily describe the same thing at the same moment. Someone might be talking about an object that isn’t on screen, for example. So simply pairing frames with a transcript can give the model misleading supervision. The challenge is selecting useful clips and aligning the information across modalities while preserving the temporal context.

r001.rationale: The response discusses aligning video with speech and text, but it does not say video corpora have less rich accompanying language than interleaved image-text corpora.
